most common clouds in the Arctic are mixed-phase clouds

, which contain both ice crystals and supercooled liquid water droplets. During the Arctic summer, when sunlight is constant, these clouds reflect sunlight back into space like a parasol, helping to cool the region. In contrast, during the long, dark Arctic winter, when there is no sunlight to reflect, the same clouds behave like a blanket, trapping heat radiated from the Earth’s surface and sending it back down to the ground.

Moving forward, the study’s findings could be used to refine climate models so that they provide a more accurate representation of the ice-to-liquid ratio within clouds and better predictions of current and future rates of Arctic warming.
Since the Arctic’s climate also plays a key role in shaping weather patterns further south, these
findings could also lead to more accurate forecasts
of extreme weather in mid-latitude regions.

“The biggest uncertainty in our forecasts is due to clouds,” concludes Michibata. “Fixing these models is essential not just for the Arctic, but for understanding its impact on weather and climate change across the globe.”
